holidays.name: National Cookie Exchange Day
holidays.description: Bakers gather to swap batches of homemade cookies so everyone ends up with a festive variety platter without baking a dozen different recipes. Come with a dozen of one kind, leave with a dozen kinds.
holidays.origin: Cookie exchanges grew out of American community and church gatherings in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and the tradition boomed in the mid-1900s as a holiday party staple. The day itself is an informal, unofficial observance.
holidays.funFact: Sweet-treat swaps have been tied to Christmas baking traditions for generations, and the Betty Crocker-era cookbooks of the 1950s helped popularize the idea of the party-sized cookie swap.

holidays.name: Forefathers' Day
holidays.description: A New England observance that commemorates the landing of the Pilgrims at Plymouth Rock, traditionally marked with dinners, speeches, and toasts to the early settlers.
holidays.origin: The Old Colony Club of Plymouth, Massachusetts began celebrating it in 1769. The date was chosen based on a calendar conversion from the Julian date of the landing, though the conversion was actually off by a day or so, which scholars later noted.
holidays.funFact: Because of a calendar-conversion mix-up, the celebration falls on December 22 rather than the date a correct conversion would give, and the tradition stuck anyway. Plymouth still marks it today.

holidays.name: Winter Solstice (Yule and Dongzhi Festival)
holidays.description: The shortest day and longest night of the year in the Northern Hemisphere, celebrated with bonfires, Yule logs, feasting, and in East Asia with dumplings and sweet rice balls.
holidays.origin: Cultures around the globe have marked the solstice for thousands of years, from Stonehenge alignments in Britain to the Chinese Dongzhi Festival, which dates back over 2,000 years and celebrates the return of longer days. The solstice usually falls on December 21 or 22.
holidays.funFact: In some parts of northern China, people eat dumplings on Dongzhi because of a legend that a physician made ear-shaped dumplings to treat villagers with frostbitten ears, and the saying goes that those who skip them may get cold ears.

holidays.name: Date Nut Bread Day
holidays.description: A day for slicing into a dense, sweet, sticky loaf studded with dates and nuts, ideally slathered with cream cheese or butter and enjoyed with tea or coffee.
holidays.origin: Date nut bread became a popular American baked good in the early 20th century, often featured in cookbooks and as a canned tea-sandwich bread. The food day is an unofficial one that is listed on December 22 in many food-holiday calendars.
holidays.funFact: Date nut bread was once so popular as a tea sandwich base that canned versions, such as the well-known B&M brown bread type of canned loaves, sat on pantry shelves alongside it as a handy emergency treat.

holidays.name: Chocolate-Covered Anything Day
holidays.description: A day dedicated to dipping absolutely anything in chocolate, from pretzels and strawberries to potato chips, bacon, and dare-you snacks of all kinds.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food celebration that came out of the holiday-snacking season, driven by candy makers and food bloggers who wanted to give chocolate lovers an excuse to experiment during the festive season.
holidays.funFact: Chocolate-covered bacon, insects, and even potato chips are real products, and the flavor combo of salty and sweet is one reason these odd dipped treats keep showing up at fairs and gourmet shops.
